narrative: A quiet, cautious young man from Aleppo had studied English literature at the University of Aleppo, where he came to love Shakespeare. When fighting came to his city in 2012 he went to Lebanon, working as a grocery-store cashier while keeping up his studies, and returned to Aleppo in December to take his final exams so he could graduate; the university sits on the regime-held side of the city, and he had not seen his home on the rebel-held side in three years. He hoped in Europe to study for a master's degree in business administration. He set out with a close friend, paying $1,000 each to a smuggler they had found on Facebook for a boat from Turkey to Greece. In a rubber dinghy with 43 people, they crossed the Aegean by daylight; not far from the island of Agathonissi the Algerian steering the boat knifed its side to keep the approaching Greek Coast Guard from pushing them back, and everyone scrambled into the shallow water as the boat sank. On Agathonissi they spent a night in a police cell, then slept on the ground outside, fed once in two and a half days, before a ferry to Samos where they waited a week for papers. They took a ferry to Athens and a train toward Macedonia, a country that repelled migrants at its border and where at least 25 people had been killed by trains while walking the tracks. Their first two attempts to cross ended in capture, detention and a truck ride back to the Greek border, with an officer threatening that next time he would beat them to death. On the third attempt they joined a group of about 70 leaving before dawn, women and children in the middle, walking silently through wheat fields, and made it across in nearly 30 hours. In Serbia they danced with other refugees to buskers at a train station. In Belgrade, when his friend ran out of money, he paid for the hotel and food for both and said he would stay until they could go on together. From Kanjiza the group of eight bused toward the border, then hiked along train tracks through paprika fields, hiding in shrubs until dark and turning off their phones; some carried box cutters against thieves. They crossed into Hungary undetected, paid $140 each for a ride to Budapest, then $1,345 each for a man to drive them toward Germany. Dropped just across the Austrian border, they walked an hour to Passau and bought tickets to Hamburg before a police officer spotted them at the station. The officer gave them fruit and told them to apply for asylum; the next morning another officer woke them as gently as a concierge. He had hoped to reach Luxembourg or the Netherlands, but the officers were so kind that they decided to stay in Germany, settling at an asylum center in Freyung, Bavaria.
